What does evidence-based healthcare use population research to inform?
column2:
Decisions about individual patients, with benefits and harms interpreted in their clinical context.

PDF p. 20

column1: What are the five broad steps of evidence-based practice?
column2:
Formulate an answerable question; find evidence; appraise validity and usefulness; implement; evaluate performance.

PDF p. 21

column1: Why is critical appraisal alone insufficient?
column2:
The question and source must fit the problem, and valid findings must be implemented and evaluated.

PDF p. 22

column1: What four components make a focused intervention question?
column2:
Population, intervention, comparison and outcomes that matter; the manoeuvre may instead be an exposure or test.

PDF p. 31

column1: Why can a factual essay fail to solve a patient's problem?
column2:
It may describe a condition without isolating the practical decision and information the patient needs.

PDF p. 30

column1: Why must patient preferences enter question formulation?
column2:
The relevant outcome and acceptable trade-offs depend on the particular patient's circumstances and values.

PDF p. 31

column1: What three purposes shape a literature search?
column2:
Browsing to keep current, answering a focused clinical question, and comprehensively surveying a research topic.

PDF p. 35

column1: When can a focused clinical search reasonably stop?
column2:
When trustworthy, relevant information has been found; this is different from an exhaustive research review.

PDF p. 36

column1: Why is a single simple database query inadequate for a comprehensive review?
column2:
A review needs systematic searching of relevant databases and citation chaining, usually with an information professional.

PDF p. 36

column1: What can a systematic review inherit from its primary studies?
column2:
Their methodological or design flaws; synthesis does not automatically remove those flaws.

PDF p. 38

column1: How can secondary sources help locate primary research?
column2:
Their references and hyperlinks provide routes to relevant original studies.

PDF p. 42

column1: What is the attraction of a federated search engine?
column2:
It searches several types of evidence resource at once; search convenience still does not establish evidence quality.

PDF p. 44

column1: What three preliminary questions orient a paper appraisal?
column2:
Why was the study needed and what was the question; what was the design; and was that design appropriate to the question?

PDF p. 51

column1: What distinguishes a randomised controlled trial?
column2:
Participants are allocated by a random process to comparison groups and followed for prespecified outcomes.

PDF p. 53

column1: Does having a control group prove a study was randomised?
column2:
No. Allocation can be non-random even when an intervention and control group are compared.

PDF p. 54

column1: Why might qualitative methods be needed when evaluating care?
column2:
Patients may value aspects of an experience that standard numerical outcomes do not capture.

PDF p. 57

column1: What is the starting point of a case-control study?
column2:
Select people with a condition and suitable controls, then investigate previous exposures.

PDF p. 59

column1: Why is an RCT not the best design for every question?
column2:
RCTs are particularly suited to intervention questions; other questions require other designs or methods.

PDF p. 55

column1: Why inspect recruitment and exclusion criteria?
column2:
They determine who was studied and whether findings can reasonably apply to the people you care for.

PDF p. 66

column1: Why distinguish recorded care from actual care?
column2:
Medical records or self-reports may measure documentation or stated behaviour rather than what happened.

PDF p. 67

column1: What should a validated outcome measure demonstrate?
column2:
That it measures the intended construct and that changes reasonably reflect changes in the patient's status.

PDF p. 68

column1: Why does randomisation not end the search for bias?
column2:
Bias can still enter through recruitment, allocation procedures, follow-up or assessment.

PDF p. 69

column1: What is the purpose of blinded assessment?
column2:
Reduce the influence of knowledge or expectations about treatment allocation on outcome assessment.

PDF p. 73

column1: Why examine statistical power before accepting a negative result?
column2:
A study may be too small to detect an important difference; absence of statistical significance need not establish no effect.

PDF p. 74

column1: What should be examined in baseline group characteristics?
column2:
Whether groups differ in important prognostic factors and whether appropriate adjustments were considered.

PDF p. 84

column1: When are observations paired?
column2:
When measurements are linked, such as before-and-after observations on the same individual.

PDF p. 90

column1: Why is a two-sided test generally appropriate?
column2:
An intervention can plausibly improve or worsen the outcome unless a one-direction assumption is convincingly justified.

PDF p. 91

column1: Why is a non-significant p-value not proof of no difference?
column2:
The study may lack enough information to detect a difference; significance alone cannot distinguish this from no effect.

PDF p. 94

column1: What do confidence intervals add to a point estimate?
column2:
They describe precision and the range of effect sizes compatible with the estimate under the model.

PDF p. 95

column1: Why express benefit in absolute as well as relative terms?
column2:
Relative reductions can obscure baseline risk; absolute effects and numbers needed to treat put benefit into context.

PDF p. 97

column1: What is a clinical trial of a simple intervention?
column2:
An evaluation of a well-defined intervention, often comparing it with a control or alternative treatment.

PDF p. 101

column1: Why examine the comparator in a drug trial?
column2:
An inappropriate alternative, dose or schedule can make the new intervention appear more favourable.

PDF p. 106

column1: Why inspect patient selection in a treatment trial?
column2:
The benefit-harm balance may not transfer to patients with different characteristics or comorbidities.

PDF p. 106

column1: What is a surrogate endpoint?
column2:
An intermediate measure used in place of a more directly patient-important outcome; its predictive validity needs evidence.

PDF p. 107

column1: Why can a plausible surrogate mislead?
column2:
Changing a marker need not produce the expected benefit in clinical outcomes, particularly if other effects intervene.

PDF p. 110

column1: Why can an efficacy RCT miss rare serious harms?
column2:
Trials powered for common efficacy outcomes are often too small to detect events occurring only once in many thousands.

PDF p. 113

column1: Why develop and pilot a complex intervention before definitive testing?
column2:
To refine components and identify acceptability, feasibility and operational problems.

PDF p. 119

column1: What distinguishes core from adaptable components?
column2:
Core elements should remain consistent; non-core elements can be adapted to local context based on development work.

PDF p. 121

column1: Why describe the control package in detail?
column2:
Otherwise differences may arise from co-interventions, such as human contact, rather than the component being credited.

PDF p. 122

column1: What should a theory of action explain?
column2:
How the intervention's components are expected to produce the intended outcomes.

PDF p. 122

column1: What does a process evaluation investigate?
column2:
How implementation occurred, fidelity to the plan, practical barriers and participant or staff experiences.

PDF p. 124

column1: Why does one negative complex-intervention trial not refute every adaptation?
column2:
The package may be poorly optimised or implemented, and effects may depend on setting and component delivery.

PDF p. 120

column1: What is sensitivity?
column2:
The proportion of people with the target condition who test positive: true positives divided by all with the condition.

PDF p. 131

column1: What is specificity?
column2:
The proportion without the target condition who test negative: true negatives divided by all without the condition.

PDF p. 131

column1: What does positive predictive value ask?
column2:
Among people with a positive result, what proportion truly have the condition? It depends on the population's disease prevalence.

PDF p. 133

column1: Why must the reference standard be independent of the new test?
column2:
Including the new test in the reference definition can make validation circular and bias accuracy estimates.

PDF p. 135

column1: What is verification or work-up bias?
column2:
Accuracy is distorted when receipt of the reference standard depends on the index test result, such as verifying positives only.

PDF p. 136

column1: How is a likelihood ratio used to update diagnostic probability?
column2:
Convert pre-test probability to odds, multiply by the appropriate likelihood ratio, then convert post-test odds to probability.

PDF p. 139

column1: Why can a narrative selection of supportive studies mislead?
column2:
Selective inclusion may reflect the reviewer's prior beliefs rather than the full eligible evidence.

PDF p. 148

column1: Why define a review question precisely before selecting papers?
column2:
It supports explicit, reproducible inclusion decisions about population, intervention, comparison and outcome.

PDF p. 151

column1: Why appraise risk of bias in included studies?
column2:
Pooling does not remove weaknesses of primary studies, and composite quality scores can obscure important differences.

PDF p. 154

column1: What is meta-analysis?
column2:
Statistical synthesis of numerical results from several studies addressing the same question, when combining them is appropriate.

PDF p. 156

column1: What does a forest plot show?
column2:
Individual study effects and uncertainty alongside an overall estimate; interpret the effect scale and no-effect line.

PDF p. 158

column1: What is heterogeneity in a review?
column2:
Differences among study results that require examination of clinical, methodological and statistical explanations.

PDF p. 161

column1: What three broad aspects of a guideline deserve appraisal?
column2:
Its content, the process used to develop it, and how it is presented to intended users.

PDF p. 174

column1: What does stakeholder involvement in guideline appraisal include?
column2:
Relevant professionals, views and preferences of the target population, and clearly identified intended users.

PDF p. 175

column1: Why inspect conflicts of interest in guideline development?
column2:
Financial and professional commitments can influence which problems are framed and which options are favoured.

PDF p. 176

column1: What expertise should a guideline panel draw on?
column2:
Topic expertise, evidence-methods expertise and the experience of people affected by the condition.

PDF p. 177

column1: How should a recommendation connect to evidence?
column2:
Through a transparent search and appraisal of relevant research, with uncertainty and evidence strength made clear.

PDF p. 178

column1: Why assess patient acceptability and practical feasibility?
column2:
An apparently sound recommendation may be unaffordable, burdensome or unacceptable to the people expected to follow it.

PDF p. 180

column1: When is cost-minimisation analysis appropriate?
column2:
When compared interventions have equivalent outcomes; otherwise simply choosing the cheapest can mislead.

PDF p. 184

column1: Why use economic modelling in addition to a single trial?
column2:
A model can compare more options and longer-term consequences, but its assumptions and input evidence need appraisal.

PDF p. 186

column1: What does a quality-adjusted life-year combine?
column2:
Time lived and a preference-based quality weight for that health state; the valuation method and whose values are used matter.

PDF p. 188

column1: What does an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio compare?
column2:
The difference in costs divided by the difference in effects between alternatives, rather than their separate average ratios.

PDF p. 189

column1: Why state an economic evaluation's perspective?
column2:
It determines whose costs and benefits are included, such as the health service, patient or society.

PDF p. 192

column1: Why perform a sensitivity analysis?
column2:
To see whether reasonable changes in uncertain assumptions or inputs change the economic conclusion.

PDF p. 194

column1: What kinds of material can qualitative research analyse?
column2:
Interviews, observations, documents and other meaning-rich data to develop explanations and understanding.

PDF p. 200

column1: What is reflexivity?
column2:
Explicit consideration of how the researcher's perspective and role may shape data collection, interpretation and claims.

PDF p. 201

column1: What is triangulation?
column2:
Bringing more than one method or perspective to bear on a question to enrich and test interpretation.

PDF p. 201

column1: What is progressive focusing?
column2:
Refining the research question and methods as emerging findings clarify what needs investigation.

PDF p. 202

column1: Why use purposive sampling?
column2:
To seek relevant and contrasting experiences that illuminate the question, rather than merely estimate an average population value.

PDF p. 205

column1: Why actively examine contradictory or negative cases?
column2:
A defensible analysis must test and refine explanations rather than cherry-pick appealing quotations.

PDF p. 207

column1: Is a questionnaire intrinsically quantitative or qualitative?
column2:
Neither; the questions and response formats determine the types of data collected.

PDF p. 215

column1: Why look for a suitable previously validated instrument?
column2:
It can save development work, enable comparisons and provide prior measurement evidence; suitability for the current use still matters.

PDF p. 217

column1: How do validity and reliability differ?
column2:
Validity concerns measuring the intended construct; reliability concerns consistency of measurement.

PDF p. 218

column1: What instructions help participants answer appropriately?
column2:
Explain purpose, confidentiality, voluntariness, contact details and how to complete each item.

PDF p. 219

column1: Why can an opening-hours survey of current clinic attenders mislead?
column2:
People unable to attend at those hours are systematically missing from the sample.

PDF p. 221

column1: Why pilot a questionnaire?
column2:
To identify problems in wording, layout and completion before the main survey and improve its practical usability.

PDF p. 222

column1: What does context mean in quality improvement?
column2:
The local organisational and real-world conditions in which a change is introduced.

PDF p. 230

column1: Why make the mechanism of improvement explicit?
column2:
It explains how a proposed change is expected to improve care and helps interpret success or failure.

PDF p. 231

column1: Why define success before evaluating an initiative?
column2:
Without specified outcomes and reasonable measurement, claims of improvement are difficult to assess.

PDF p. 232

column1: Why report the change process in detail?
column2:
Who did what, how and under what constraints helps others interpret outcomes and transfer lessons.

PDF p. 233

column1: What is the Hawthorne effect relevant to quality improvement?
column2:
Performance can change because staff receive attention or know a change is being studied, not solely because of its intrinsic content.

PDF p. 234

column1: What distinguishes local improvement from a broader research claim?
column2:
Research claims need justified lessons transferable beyond the local site, with context and limitations explained.

PDF p. 236

column1: What is a genome-wide association study?
column2:
A large observational study comparing genomic variants in relation to traits or disease, often using cohort or case-control designs.

PDF p. 241

column1: Why is a disease-associated SNP not automatically causal?
column2:
It can mark an associated genomic region without itself being the causal variant; biological plausibility needs further investigation.

PDF p. 243

column1: Does a risk-associated variant predict inevitable disease?
column2:
No. Many associations are weak and probabilistic, so an association is not a deterministic individual prediction.

PDF p. 244

column1: Why do observational quality checks still matter in GWAS?
column2:
Case and control selection, population differences, confounding and measurement can still distort high-technology studies.

PDF p. 250

column1: Why define phenotypes precisely?
column2:
Inconsistent or unclear disease and trait definitions can undermine genetic association analyses.

PDF p. 251

column1: What is the winner's curse?
column2:
Initially detected associations can have inflated effect estimates because larger apparent effects more readily cross significance thresholds.

PDF p. 252

column1: How do patient narrative and research evidence relate?
column2:
They can complement one another: population evidence informs care while the patient's story and clinical judgement give individual meaning.

PDF p. 257

column1: What are patient-reported outcome measures?
column2:
Instruments collecting outcomes directly from patients, intended to capture aspects of health that matter to them.

PDF p. 258

column1: What does shared decision-making support?
column2:
A supported deliberation between clinician and patient about evidence, options, uncertainty and the patient's priorities.

PDF p. 259

column1: What is an option grid designed to do?
column2:
Support a focused comparison and conversation about options using questions important to patients.

PDF p. 262

column1: Why does an option grid need conversation?
column2:
Its purpose is option talk and deliberation, not merely handing over information.

PDF p. 263

column1: What practical limitation can affect n-of-1 trials?
column2:
Repeated switches and trial participation may be burdensome; people may prefer to continue an option they feel works.

PDF p. 265

column1: What distinguishes machine learning from fixed rules?
column2:
Algorithms learn patterns from data rather than relying solely on explicitly programmed decision rules.

PDF p. 273

column1: Why check fluent generative-AI output?
column2:
Conversational fluency and apparent confidence do not establish factual correctness or clinical reliability.

PDF p. 274

column1: What is the first practical AI appraisal question?
column2:
Its intended use, intended users, target patients and relevance to the clinical problem.

PDF p. 279

column1: What should be reported about AI input data?
column2:
Their source, acquisition, preprocessing, quality and handling of missing or poor-quality inputs.

PDF p. 281

column1: Why is AI safety assessment continuous?
column2:
Risks can emerge before, during and after implementation; changes and observed harms need reporting.

PDF p. 282

column1: Why might study performance not transfer to practice?
column2:
Local patients, workflow and implementation may differ from the training and evaluation setting.

PDF p. 277

column1: What is mechanistic evidence?
column2:
Evidence about the causal process through which an intervention or exposure produces an effect.

PDF p. 287

column1: How can mechanisms explain a failed feeding programme?
column2:
Food may not be eaten, absorbed or delivered as expected; local biological and social pathways can block effects.

PDF p. 288

column1: Are mechanistic studies equally strong?
column2:
No. Their quality and contribution to a coherent causal explanation need appraisal; a simple hierarchy is insufficient.

PDF p. 289

column1: How do mechanisms and probabilistic evidence contribute together?
column2:
They address complementary aspects of causal inference, including observed associations and causal pathways.

PDF p. 290

column1: What does EBM+ add to appraisal?
column2:
Consider mechanistic alongside probabilistic evidence rather than treating either as a universal substitute.

PDF p. 291

column1: Why distinguish advice from actual exposure?
column2:
If advice does not change behaviour, its effect does not establish the effect of consistently receiving the intervention.

PDF p. 294

column1: What are four key Delphi characteristics?
column2:
Anonymity, iteration, feedback and statistical analysis of responses.

PDF p. 303

column1: How does nominal group technique broaden participation?
column2:
Structured individual idea generation and turn-taking reduce domination of initial contributions by outspoken people.

PDF p. 302

column1: What expertise can enrich a consensus panel?
column2:
Research-methods, clinical and lived-experience expertise, with relevant perspectives represented.

PDF p. 306

column1: Why describe and justify the consensus method?
column2:
Readers need to judge fit with the question, modifications and the definition of consensus.

PDF p. 307

column1: Why examine stability between Delphi rounds?
column2:
It shows whether agreement or disagreement persists or changes and can identify enduring tensions.

PDF p. 308

column1: Why report dissent?
column2:
Minority views and their reasons may matter to decisions; agreement percentages can conceal substantive disagreement.

PDF p. 309

column1: How can poor evidence-based practice fail its own aims?
column2:
By treating numbers uncritically, imposing rigid protocols or disregarding patients rather than applying evidence thoughtfully.

PDF p. 313

column1: Why is missing trial evidence not proof that a need is unimportant?
column2:
Published research does not map perfectly onto patient needs or all forms of useful knowledge.

PDF p. 314

column1: What concern accompanies excessive standardisation?
column2:
Rules can impose unjustified control and fail to reflect clinical complexity.

PDF p. 315

column1: Why can an average effect miss an individual's priorities?
column2:
The patient's experience is a complex story that may not fit a population average or one utility score.

PDF p. 316

column1: Why can accumulating guidelines create problems?
column2:
The volume of recommendations can exceed what clinicians can absorb or use appropriately in a consultation.

PDF p. 317

column1: Why does policy require more than evidence of what works?
column2:
Decisions involve values, priorities, context and socially agreed goals as well as effects.

PDF p. 319

column1: What begins a context-sensitive evidence-based encounter?
column2:
Identify and prioritise clinical, psychological, social and other concerns, including the patient's perspective.

PDF p. 323

column1: What determines the search strategy in the checklist?
column2:
Whether the purpose is browsing, a focused answer or a comprehensive review.

PDF p. 324

column1: How should design be judged in general appraisal?
column2:
Against the research question and field, alongside ethics and governance.

PDF p. 325

column1: What should be considered before accepting a pooled result?
column2:
The question, search, quality assessment, missing data and whether combining results is reasonable.

PDF p. 328

column1: What should a decision aid communicate besides options?
column2:
Relevant outcomes and probabilities, uncertainty, preference support, sources and possible conflicts of interest.

PDF p. 332

column1: Why appraise rather than merely name mechanistic evidence?
column2:
Its type, relevance and quality determine its contribution to the causal account.

PDF p. 333

column1: How is control event rate calculated?
column2:
Control participants with the event divided by all control participants: a/(a+b).

PDF p. 335

column1: How is experimental event rate calculated?
column2:
Experimental participants with the event divided by all experimental participants: c/(c+d).

PDF p. 335

column1: How is relative risk calculated?
column2:
Experimental event rate divided by control event rate, provided control event rate is nonzero.

PDF p. 335

column1: How is absolute risk reduction calculated for an undesirable event?
column2:
Control event rate minus experimental event rate; use proportions and preserve the outcome and time horizon.

PDF p. 335

column1: How is relative risk reduction calculated?
column2:
Derived from the relative-risk formula: RRR = 1 − RR = (CER − EER)/CER, when CER is nonzero. This is an authored algebraic explanation of the source formulas.

PDF p. 335

column1: How is NNT calculated for a positive absolute risk reduction?
column2:
The reciprocal of absolute risk reduction expressed as a proportion, for the specified outcome and follow-up period.

PDF p. 335

column1: What should remain independent before consulting AI?
column2:
Your decision question and initial interpretation, so the generated response can be compared with a human starting point. This is an authored learning workflow, not a validated anti-bias guarantee.

Evidence context: https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.241776

column1: What two checks does a citation require?
column2:
Verify that the reference exists and that its actual content supports the specific claim.

Evidence context: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12935541/

column1: What should happen when the supplied excerpt omits a method?
column2:
Record it as unreported in the supplied material and seek the relevant full methods, protocol or supplement; do not fill the gap by assumption.

Evidence context: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12644243/

column1: How should AI-extracted numbers be checked?
column2:
Compare event, numerator, denominator, units and time horizon with the original table, then independently recalculate.

Evidence context: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12644243/

column1: Does retrieval-backed output establish a complete literature search?
column2:
No. Discovery coverage and source selection still need methods appropriate to the question.

Evidence context: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12935541/; https://www.cochrane.org/about-us/news/cochrane-launches-innovative-study-assess-ai-tools-evidence-synthesis

column1: What belongs in an AI assistance log?
column2:
Tool/version, date, task, supplied material, prompt, retrieval scope, output checks and corrections; follow the relevant reporting policy.

Evidence context: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12644243/; https://www.icmje.org/recommendations/browse/artificial-intelligence/ai-use-by-authors.html

column1: Can a confidential manuscript be uploaded merely because you are its reviewer?
column2:
No. Follow journal policy; when confidentiality cannot be assured, explicit author permission is required before such sharing.

Evidence context: https://www.icmje.org/recommendations/browse/artificial-intelligence/ai-use-by-editors.html

column1: Who retains responsibility for a submitted AI-assisted appraisal?
column2:
The human author or reviewer; AI does not take responsibility for accuracy, attribution or interpretation.

Evidence context: https://www.icmje.org/recommendations/browse/artificial-intelligence/ai-use-by-authors.html
